title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows a general-purpose AI coding agent, Cursor Agent running Claude Sonnet, being used as an operational tool inside an active ransomware campaign. The failure is not a model producing false output or being deceived into a harmful response in isolation. It is a case of a legitimate productivity tool being repurposed wholesale for hands-on network exploitation, with the AI assisting attackers in conducting intrusions against real organizations. The deployment context the tool was built for, software development, was simply discarded by the operators.

The gap that allowed this is the absence of any mechanism to distinguish malicious use from legitimate use at the point of operation. Cursor Agent executed tasks against live victim infrastructure because it was capable of doing so and nothing in its deployment stopped it. Catching this would have required either behavioral monitoring capable of flagging exploitation-pattern commands issued through the agent, or restrictions on the environments and network contexts in which the agent could act. Neither is established as having been in place.

What is not established is whether Anysphere, the company behind Cursor, had any knowledge of this use, whether any safeguard was attempted and bypassed, or whether the attribution of both activity clusters to Aurora ransomware with certainty rather than medium confidence for the second cluster is a final finding rather than a research assessment.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments and is operating a data leak site. The group used Cursor Agent, which runs Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation against ten organizations between April and May 2026. The ESXi ransomware encrypts virtual machine files using ChaCha20 encryption while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands. Aurora operators also deployed custom tools like esxi_finder.py to scan networks for VMware infrastructure.

Researchers identified a second cluster of Aurora activity with medium confidence, affecting eight victim organizations across multiple countries including Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. This cluster used different techniques, including SQL Server exploitation and DCSync attacks for lateral movement and data exfiltration to self-hosted S3 storage. Gambit Security provided indicators of compromise including IP addresses, domains, and file hashes to help organizations identify and defend against Aurora ransomware operations.
